data.title: A voyage by Roman ship down the Danube – part 2
data.excerpt: The second part of the report from a voyage by Roman ship down the Danube. The crew put in at the forts of the Pannonian limes – Matrica, Intercisa, Bölcske, Lussonium and Alta Ripa – and Hungarian towns welcomed them with drums, Roman soldiers in full armour and festivals.
data.metaTitle: A voyage by Roman ship down the Danube – part 2
data.metaDescription: The second part of the report from a voyage by Roman ship down the Danube: the Pannonian forts of Matrica, Intercisa, Lussonium and Alta Ripa.

children.text: The continuation of the first part of the
report from the voyage by Roman ship
Matrica

Our journey continued to the next stop, Matrica. An ancient Roman military camp stood here, with a civilian settlement built beside it, in the province of Pannonia. The fort was built beside the main road running along the Danube south of Aquincum. According to a 3rd-century itinerary (the Itinerarium Antonini) it lay 23 Roman miles from Aquincum, that is at a distance of about 33 kilometres. Its remains were found in the present-day town of Százhalombatta. The identity of the site and of the name in the description is confirmed by the find of a brick and by an inscription on an altar stone. When Pannonia was divided (at the beginning of the 2nd century), Matrica came under the province of Pannonia Inferior, and after Diocletian’s administrative reform (at the end of the 3rd century) it was part of Pannonia Valeria. The Celtic tribe of the Eravisci lived in the surroundings of the camp. The Romans took control of the Danube line in the first half of the 1st century. The founding of Matrica can be dated to the first half of the 2nd century, under the rule of Trajan or Hadrian. The fortification was originally of timber and earth, and after the fort was destroyed in the war against the Sarmatians around 178 it was rebuilt using stone. The work was carried out by the unit stationed here, the cohors milliaria Maurorum. This infantry unit, recruited in the African province of Mauretania, consisted of 1,000 men. In the 3rd century a 300-strong cavalry corps, the Equites promoti, was quartered in the camp, but by the 4th century its number had been reduced to 100–200 men. Because of the increasingly frequent barbarian raids in the 4th century, the population of the settlement also moved into the area of the camp. At the beginning of the 5th century, however, the camp was taken over by the Huns. The fort survived in relatively good condition, because the Danube floods spared it. Great damage, however, was done by building work in 1809, when earth ramparts and bastions were raised on its area during the Napoleonic wars. The stone walls of the camp, which measures 152 × 155 metres, are 90–140 cm thick. A double ditch ran in front of the walls. The north–south main road (via principalis) running through the rectangular military camp was paved with stone slabs. The headquarters building (principia) stood in the centre of the camp, where the two main roads crossed at right angles. The other streets, too, showed a regular layout. The headquarters building could be entered from the east, through a colonnade. In the south-eastern part of its courtyard there was a well, which was also lined with stone slabs. Around the building stood, in military order, workshops, storehouses and stables, as well as the soldiers’ quarters. The emperor’s statues and the battle standards were kept in the camp sanctuary, but this has been only partly investigated.

The walls of the fort were built by a method common under the rule of Commodus. This meant that its gate towers projected by a third and that its corner towers also projected beyond the line of the wall. The semicircular corner tower may have been built later, in the time of Caracalla. Recent excavation has also revealed the north-western corner tower of fan-shaped form. In a later period (the 4th century) the fort ditch was filled in, because its walls were strengthened with far-projecting side and corner towers, and further ditches were dug beyond them. The remains of a watchtower (burgus) were found 2.5 km south of the camp and in the camp, which was built in 185. The military camp was surrounded on the north, west and south by a civilian settlement (vicus militaris, a “camp village”). Its extent reached 400 × 900 metres. The soldiers’ family members lived here, and so did craftsmen, manufacturers, traders and their families, who supplied the army. At the beginning the huts were sunk into the ground; during the 2nd century stone buildings were also erected in an ever greater number of places, especially in the parts towards the camp. The excavations uncovered the foundations of 23 features of the settlement, and in 1995 a further 29 features were found. The most interesting of them is the bath building, which has three hot (caldarium), one warm (tepidarium) and two cold (frigidarium) pools. The remains of most of the houses (frescoes, stuccoes, column capitals) have survived only in poor condition.  A cemetery of the military camp grew up along the main roads. In the southern cemetery, 213 graves were excavated in connection with the construction of the DKV reservoir, although more than a hundred may remain uninvestigated. The number of graves destroyed before the rescue work began can be estimated at a thousand. Cremation cemeteries were found from the earlier period (the 1st–2nd centuries) and, from the middle of the 2nd century, mainly inhumation cemeteries. The dead were mostly laid in the ground; sometimes the grave was lined with bricks, or was lined with bricks entirely. Burials in sarcophagi are rarer still. The grave goods include vessels (for example the valuable terra sigillata pottery), small bottles, candlesticks and perfumes. Swords and knives beside the men, brooches beside the women, together with bracelets, earrings or pearls. The coins found in the graves range from the middle of the 1st century to the end of the 4th century. From the 4th century cremation burial was no longer practised and no grave goods were placed in the inhumation graves. In the case of wealthier people, gravestones were also erected, and these provide important information about the composition and the way of life of the population. The northern and western cemeteries have been less extensively excavated. They contain built graves with skeletons, and two burial chambers were also discovered. Besides those mentioned so far, milestones along the roads, altar stones and inscriptions on buildings have also come to light. These were placed in the lapidarium of the Matrica Museum in Százhalombatta, where they can be visited today. The town of Százhalombatta surprised me. The welcome programme was extraordinarily beautiful: we sailed into the harbour escorted by boats and to the sound of drums beating to the rhythm of the oar strokes. Roman soldiers in full armour were waiting on the bank, and our landing was accompanied by enthusiastic applause and cheering. Seriously, to experience such a welcome is to be filled with emotion and energy. The archaeological park was a huge surprise, but that belongs to a different historical period.

children.text: Intercisa

The town of Dunaújváros attracts attention with the settlement of Intercisa, which was built within the defensive system along the Danube basin, the Limes Pannonicus, that is the land frontier erected in Roman times. It was our next stop.

It entered local history as the fort of Intercisa (castrum), a watchtower on the bank of the Danube. In Roman times this place was the seat of a legion. Along the Danube such fortifications stood in a row one after another: Annamatia (Baracs), Lussonium (Paks) and, to the north, Campona (Nagytéteny), after which the shopping centre was also named. These fortifications were built one after another at fairly regular intervals.

The earliest camp was founded south of the later one, but only a short fortified stretch of it is known. The palanquin camp of the first period beneath the stone fort was built in the time of Trajan; its width is 165 m, but its length cannot be determined precisely because of the shoreline: it can be estimated at roughly 190 m. On the front of the retentura the wall was supported by a double row of props, into which turf bricks were also set. In one stretch on the southern side only a turf-brick wall was found. The stone fort was built at the end of and after the Marcomannic war, and its roughly 1.2 m thick foundation wall was placed on the outer edge of the ditch of the palanquin camp. The distance between the old and the new defensive line was chosen so that the new soil dug out of the ditch, which was considerably wider and deeper than the previous one, would yield the amount of earth needed to build the agger. Because of the risk of collapse, its western wall was shifted 20 m to the west, but the side gates remained where they had been before. A narrowed part of the ditch of the palanquin camp was found here, a single-gate tower of the southern gate of the stone fort resting on four wooden posts, and then a double tower with a stone gate from the rebuilding carried out in the time of Caracalla. The porta decumana and the porta principalis sinistra were also similar, but it is possible that the porta praetoria was not built at the edge of the slope at all. The size of the slightly rhomboid bailey was 176 × about 200 m. The second rebuilding of the fort probably took place in the time of the emperor Constantine, in the Late Roman period. Fan-shaped towers were built at the corners, and the porta decumana was closed and converted into a horseshoe-shaped tower. On the inner side of the fort wall a tower was built in place of the demolished agger. After the previous ditch had been filled in, the new defensive ditch was laid out considerably further out. The last building period can be dated to the time of Gratian and Theodosius. The fort was still in use in the first decades of the 5th century – partly by the Foederati, who were settling there – but then it was abandoned.

children.text: Bölcske

Between 1986 and 2004 an archaeological excavation was carried out at Bölcske, during which a Roman bridgehead dated to the third quarter of the 4th century was found. The uniqueness of the site lay in the discovery of the bridgehead structures under water in the Danube; the excavation here was the first major undertaking of underwater archaeology in Hungary. At first the excavation used a special crane mounted on a boat, which lifted some architectural elements, thanks to which it was confirmed that they came mainly from the Roman town of Aquincum (modern Budapest). This meant that the researchers who began fieldwork at the site had to pass diving examinations, and with the help of other divers it became possible, several years after the research project began, to survey the site with a newly available survey device (the Seistec sonar), which used a system similar to GPS and was able to work under water from a boat.

children.text: Lussonium

Lussonium is an archaeological site and an ancient Roman fort built on the frontier of the province of Pannonia, on the bank of the Danube. It lies near the town of Dunakömlőd in Hungary. Unlike other areas, where extensive frontier fortifications were built, such as Hadrian’s Wall in Britain or the great earth ramparts and palisades of the Limes Germanicus, the Danubian limes was strengthened by a network of numerous watchtowers, legionary camps (castra) and forts (castella).

The find of decorated Roman pottery at Lussonium – terra sigillata and terra nigra in situ – indicates that Lussonium was built as a castrum during the 1st century AD, under the rule of the emperor Claudius or Nero. The fort went through three main building phases; the first phase consisted of timber and earth and underwent various alterations until the end of the Marcomannic wars. The second phase, around the end of the 3rd and the beginning of the 4th century AD, replaced the timber structures and defences with a stone fort. In the third phase, at the end of the 4th century AD, this stone fort was destroyed and replaced by a smaller fort with timber structures and a large stone tower.

blocks.alt: A voyage by Roman ship down the Danube – part 2

children.text: Lussonium was held by the garrison of the Cohors I Alpinorum equitata, a cohort of 500–1,000 soldiers. The soldiers were assigned here to defend the frontier against the warlike Sarmatian tribes of the Iazyges, who lived on the opposite banks of the Danube. A vicus settlement (an ad hoc provincial civilian settlement) grew up around the fort, which probably served the nearby villa farms and the Romanised native villages in the surroundings as a centre of agricultural trade.

In the past, as a result of a change in the course of the Danube and the gradual weathering of the rock, about half of this fort slid away; today half of the occupation lies buried beneath the present-day village of Dunakömlőd.

The Paks-Lussonium archaeological park lies a short distance from the town of Paks, on a steep, narrow hill overlooking the floodplains along the banks of the Danube. When you stand on the reconstruction of the timber tower of the entrance gate and see the broad space before you, you imagine the buildings, the soldiers, the horses… the life that may once have gone on here, as in a film. Paks is a very modern town, and there is a wonderful museum here.

children.text: Alta Ripa (Tolna)

The history of the village of Tolna goes back to Roman times. Along the bank of the Danube stretched the limes already mentioned above, the system of Roman frontier defensive forts. The harbour and the customs house were guarded by a castellum called “Alta Ripa”. It was a settlement of military character, and only after the collapse of the Roman Empire did it become possible for the place to turn into a civilian settlement, when the uninhabited buildings passed into the possession of various ethnic groups (the Slavs, the Avars, the Hungarians). After the formation of the Kingdom of Hungary the settlement was occupied again, which also confirmed the importance of the Tolna ferry. In those times the surroundings of Tolna and Kalocsa served as winter quarters for the sons and grandsons of the ruling princes.

The voyage down the Danube, however, was not only about Rome. Besides museums we experienced a host of interesting programmes. In Százhalombatta we, as the crew, were guests of honour at a folklore festival; in Dunaújváros a festival of modern music was held; in Dunaföldvár a rowing club welcomed us like friends of many years. In Madocsa and Bölcske we were entertained like close relatives, and I could go on like this for a long time. In Hungary I met with hospitality and a friendly welcome. In the evening people danced together in a circle in the square, holding hands and laughing. No one looked at anyone else with misgiving or fear. I rather miss such kind-heartedness and joy here in Slovakia. One of the greatest surprises was the town of Baja. The historic centre is beautiful, tiny restaurants offer tasty food and there are flowers everywhere. In Baja you will also find a
museum awarded the title of Museum of the Year

. Since January 2020 a new permanent exhibition has awaited visitors in the museum. The whole two weeks were demanding, not only physically but also mentally. Complete strangers who had signed up as volunteer rowers became friends who helped one another to overcome discomfort, high temperatures and rain as well. We adapted to one another and bore with one another… It sounds almost unbelievable, but the farewell was full of hugs, gratitude and laughter.

blocks.alt: A voyage by Roman ship down the Danube – part 2

children.text: We greeted every town with our rallying cry. We hailed every crew on every boat that sailed past us with the same shout… This cry became a kind of motto of our two-week adventure in “the service of Rome”. Roma aeterna, Roma invicta, Danuvina Alacris! — Rome eternal, Rome unconquered, the Danube alive! And so the voyage and the whole project will remain in my memory.
Nika
